example.answer: You will be debt-free in 33 months. You will pay $6,521.02 in total, of which $1,521.02 is interest.
example.problem: You owe $5,000 on a card with 19.99% APR and pay $200 a month. How long until the card is paid off, and what does it cost?
steps: Monthly interest on $5,000: $5,000 × 0.016658 = $83.29. Your $200 payment covers that and cuts the balance by $116.71.
Payoff time: −ln(1 − (0.016658 × $5,000 ÷ $200)) ÷ ln(1 + 0.016658) = 32.60 months, rounded up to 33 payments.
Total paid over 33 payments: $6,521.02 (the last payment is smaller than $200).
example.title: Paying off a $5,000 balance

faqs.a: Yes — dramatically. Because more of each payment attacks the balance instead of just covering interest, even $50 extra a month can cut years off a large balance. Try your numbers with a higher payment to see the difference.
faqs.q: Does paying a little extra each month really help?

faqs.a: Only paying the minimum (often 1–2% of the balance) means most of your payment feeds interest and the balance barely shrinks. A $5,000 balance at 19.99% with minimum payments can take over a decade to clear.
faqs.q: What happens if I only make minimum payments?

faqs.a: Your payment must be bigger than the monthly interest charge, or the balance grows forever. On a $5,000 balance at 19.99%, the monthly interest is $83.29 — anything at or below that never pays the card off.
faqs.q: Why does my payment have to exceed the monthly interest?

faqs.a: Yes. A balance transfer to a 0% card or a lower-rate loan reduces the monthly interest, so more of each payment cuts the balance and you finish sooner and cheaper.
faqs.q: Would a balance transfer to a lower rate help?

formula.expr: months n = −ln(1 − r × balance ÷ payment) ÷ ln(1 + r)
formula.label: Months to pay off
formula.note: Rounded up, since the last payment is a smaller one

formula.expr: total interest = total paid − starting balance
formula.label: Total interest cost
formula.note: What the debt costs you beyond what you borrowed

howItWorks: Credit card debt works like a mortgage in reverse: each month the card adds interest to your balance, then your payment first wipes out that interest and whatever is left shrinks the balance. The calculator finds how many months it takes for the balance to hit zero with your fixed payment, using the exact amortization formula rather than a rough guess.

Two totals matter. The total you pay shows the real price of the debt, and the total interest shows how much of it was pure cost above what you borrowed. Both are computed month by month, so the smaller final payment is handled correctly.

This is an estimate for planning purposes, not financial advice. It assumes the APR never changes, no new spending is added, and no fees or penalties apply. Real cards can change rates and add fees, so treat the result as a best-case guide and talk to a qualified advisor about debt problems.
intro: Find out how long it takes to pay off a credit card and what it really costs. Enter your balance, the APR, and your monthly payment to see the months to debt-free, the total you will pay, and the total interest.

mistakes.text: A 19.99% APR is 0.016658 per month, not 0.1999. Using the annual rate monthly would charge twelve times too much interest.
mistakes.title: Using the APR as the monthly rate

mistakes.text: If your payment only covers the $83.29 monthly interest on a $5,000 balance at 19.99%, the balance never moves. Pay more than the interest or the debt never shrinks.
mistakes.title: Paying only the interest each month

mistakes.text: Adding new purchases while paying off a balance is like bailing water with a leak in the boat. The calculator assumes no new spending.
mistakes.title: Adding new spending while paying down

mistakes.text: Only making minimum payments stretches a $5,000 balance at 19.99% over a decade or more, mostly feeding interest. A fixed larger payment finishes far sooner.
mistakes.title: Sticking to minimum payments
